title: UN safe-and-secure AI dialogue co-leads publish roadmap for what governments must do next
subtitle: Writing in Fortune, the co-chairs argue existing national efforts are necessary but insufficient — and lay out a small number of concrete steps they say all UN members should adopt now.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The co-leads of the United Nations' dialogue on safe and secure AI published a Fortune op-ed on September 21 arguing that current national regulatory efforts, while necessary, will not be enough on their own. They call for a small, concrete set of steps every UN member state should adopt now — incident-reporting mechanisms with shared taxonomies, common definitions of frontier-model risk, and a lightweight coordination body that can convene labs and regulators across borders.

The piece is deliberately narrow. The authors avoid the harder political questions — enforcement, trade sanctions, model bans — and focus on the coordination gaps they say already have consensus support: a country whose citizens are harmed by a model shipped elsewhere currently has no standard way to raise the incident, and labs have no standard way to warn regulators in jurisdictions they don't operate in. Their argument is that filling those gaps is achievable inside the current UN process and does not require a new treaty.

The timing tracks Xi's arrival in Washington for the Trump summit, where AI safety was just formally placed on the bilateral agenda, and last week's talks among Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind on a shared AI-safety standards body. Three tracks — UN multilateral, US-China bilateral, and industry self-organized — are all converging on the same problem: no one has a working incident-reporting pipeline for frontier models, and everyone is discovering that the ad-hoc approach breaks the first time a real incident spans borders.

A note for learners: multilateral governance always looks slow from the outside and impossibly fast from the inside. If you're following AI policy, watch which of the three tracks — UN, US-China, industry — actually publishes a common incident-reporting taxonomy first. Whichever one does will shape how every other country writes its rules, because governments will borrow the taxonomy rather than invent their own.

sources.title: We co-led the UN's dialogue on safe and secure AI. Here's what needs to happen now — Fortune
